🚀 Get started

Source: vignettes/articles/get-started.Rmd
get-started.Rmd

faofishingreport turns the FAO Global Capture Production statistics into charts, maps and tables for reports. This page walks through a complete first analysis of the Eastern Central Atlantic (FAO major fishing area 34); every chart below was produced by the code shown above it.

A typical workflow:

Step What you do Functions
1. Data Check for and download the latest FAO release check_fao_update(), download_fao_data()
2. Fishing area Total catch, main species and main countries of an area fishing_area_data(), fishing_area_species(), fishing_area_country()
3. Species and countries Who catches a species, what a country catches species_country(), country_species(), country_analysis()
4. Summaries Composition, stock status, trends, data quality, fleets stock_status(), peak_trend(), coastal_distant(), …
5. Style Language, theme, colours, map projection fao_settings()

📦 Installation

faofishingreport needs R 4.2 or later. Install it from GitHub:

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("Linbojun99/faofishingreport")

All required packages (dplyr, ggplot2, sf, rnaturalearth, …) are installed automatically.

Windows and macOS use binary packages, so no compiler (Rtools) is needed. Linux needs the system libraries of the sf package and, for Chinese charts, a Chinese font:

sudo apt-get install libgdal-dev libgeos-dev libproj-dev libudunits2-dev fonts-noto-cjk

Load the package. The start-up message shows the operating system and the font chosen for charts (SimSun on Windows, Songti SC on macOS, Noto Serif CJK SC on Linux):

library(faofishingreport)
#> faofishingreport: Windows, chart font "SimSun" (change it with fao_font())

💾 Get the latest FAO data

The package comes with FAO release 2026.1.0. FAO publishes a new release about once a year. Check whether a newer one exists and download it (about 5 MB, a few seconds):

check_fao_update()
#> FAO Global Capture Production
#>   Latest online release: 2026.1.0 (published 2026-03-30)
#>   Bundled with package:  2026.1.0
#>   Downloaded locally:    none
#>   Your data is up to date.

download_fao_data()   # only needed when a newer release is available

All functions automatically use the newest data available. See 💾 FAO data for choosing releases, the data format and working with your own subsets.

📁 Where the results go

Each analysis saves its charts and tables in the current working folder:

Folder Content
figures/png/ Charts as PNG (always)
figures/pptx/ Charts as editable PowerPoint files (with pptx = TRUE; needs the eoffice package)
tables/ Tables as CSV, readable by Excel including Chinese names

So start by choosing a folder for the report:

setwd("D:/reports/FAO34")   # any folder

🌊 First analysis: FAO area 34

fishing_area_data() extracts the catch of one FAO major fishing area and draws its total catch with the breakpoints of the mean catch, its share of the world catch, and a world map of the countries fishing there.

FAO34 <- fishing_area_data("Atlantic, Eastern Central")

The result is a list; FAO34$area_data holds the catch records of the area and is the input of most other functions:

show_table(FAO34$area_data, n = 5)
Country..Name. ASFIS.species..Name. FAO.major.fishing.area..Name. Unit..Name. Unit Year Production Production.Type
9075 Angola Soles nei Atlantic, Eastern Central Tonnes - live weight TLW, Number 1,970 0 actual
9076 Angola Soles nei Atlantic, Eastern Central Tonnes - live weight TLW, Number 1,971 0 actual
9077 Angola Soles nei Atlantic, Eastern Central Tonnes - live weight TLW, Number 1,972 0 actual
9078 Angola Soles nei Atlantic, Eastern Central Tonnes - live weight TLW, Number 1,973 97 actual
9079 Angola Soles nei Atlantic, Eastern Central Tonnes - live weight TLW, Number 1,974 0 actual

Any other area works the same way. The names of the FAO major fishing areas are:

data <- load_fao_data()
sort(unique(data$FAO.major.fishing.area..Name.))
#>  [1] "Africa - Inland waters"           "America, North - Inland waters"  
#>  [3] "America, South - Inland waters"   "Arctic Sea"                      
#>  [5] "Asia - Inland waters"             "Atlantic, Antarctic"             
#>  [7] "Atlantic, Eastern Central"        "Atlantic, Northeast"             
#>  [9] "Atlantic, Northwest"              "Atlantic, Southeast"             
#> [11] "Atlantic, Southwest"              "Atlantic, Western Central"       
#> [13] "Europe - Inland waters"           "Former USSR area - Inland waters"
#> [15] "Indian Ocean, Antarctic"          "Indian Ocean, Eastern"           
#> [17] "Indian Ocean, Western"            "Mediterranean and Black Sea"     
#> [19] "Oceania - Inland waters"          "Pacific, Antarctic"              
#> [21] "Pacific, Eastern Central"         "Pacific, Northeast"              
#> [23] "Pacific, Northwest"               "Pacific, Southeast"              
#> [25] "Pacific, Southwest"               "Pacific, Western Central"

🐟 Main species and countries

The ten species with the largest catch in area 34, their catch over time and the breakpoints of their mean catch:

species <- fishing_area_species(FAO34$area_data, rank_range = c(1, 10))

The same for the countries:

countries <- fishing_area_country(FAO34$area_data, rank_range = c(1, 10))

🌐 Chinese and bilingual charts

Every analysis has a lang argument: "en" (English), "zh" (Chinese) or "both". Country, species and area names use the official FAO Chinese names.

species_country(FAO34$area_data, species_name = "European pilchard(=Sardine)", lang = "both")

To use Chinese everywhere, set it once with fao_settings(lang = "zh").

📊 A first summary: stock status

stock_status() classifies each species by its catch relative to its peak catch:

status <- stock_status(FAO34$area_data)
